title: How to Clean Grout Without Wrecking It
metaTitle: How to Clean Grout Without Damaging It | Las Cruces Cleaning
metaDescription: Grout is porous cement, so the harsh fixes eat it. Start mild and escalate only if you have to. What to use, what to skip, and when to reseal.
summary: Most grout that looks ruined is loaded with soap film, not stained, and bleach is why it keeps coming back.
transcript: Grout is porous cement. That's the whole problem. It absorbs everything that lands on it, and the aggressive things that pull stains back out also eat the cement.
So start with the mildest thing that could work and escalate only if it doesn't. Most grout that looks hopeless is carrying soap film and body oils, not stains.
First pass is hot water and a stiff nylon brush. Nylon, not wire. Work a section about two feet square and wipe the slurry away before it dries back into the joint.

If that leaves it grey, move to an alkaline cleaner. Oxygen bleach dissolved in warm water is the workhorse. Let it sit fifteen to thirty minutes, keep it wet, then brush. Alkaline lifts oils and soap, which is what most floor and shower grout is actually holding.

Only after that, consider acid, and only on unglazed ceramic or porcelain. Acid dissolves cement, so every acid pass takes a thin layer of grout with it. Once on a bad shower is fine. Monthly and you'll have recessed, crumbling joints inside a couple of years.

Chlorine bleach is the one to skip. It whitens the surface and leaves the soil sitting there, so the joint looks fixed for a week and comes back darker. It degrades the grout as well, and it can permanently discolor colored grout. Steel wool and green pads scratch the tile around the joint. Steam works genuinely well but strips sealer, so plan to reseal after.

Dark streaks in a shower, especially along the bottom of a wall and in the corners, are usually mildew growing in the grout rather than on it, and a surface cleaner never reaches it. While you're down there, check the corners where two planes meet. Those joints should be flexible caulk. If they're grouted, the grout has cracked and water is getting behind it, and that's a repair, not a cleaning job.

Seal it once you're done and the grout is fully dry, which takes at least a day. Sealer doesn't make grout stain proof, it buys you time to wipe something up before it soaks in. Use a penetrating sealer on floors, and expect to redo a shower every year or two.
localNote: Hard water makes grout worse here in a specific way. Mineral builds up on the surface of the joint and turns it chalky and pale, and people read pale as clean while the grout underneath is still loaded. If your shower grout looks light and rough, deal with the mineral first using the vinegar method, then deal with the soil.

faq.q: Why does my grout look clean and then go grey a week later?
faq.a: Almost always bleach. It lightens what's on top without removing it. Switch to an oxygen bleach soak and a nylon brush.

faq.q: Can I use a steam cleaner?
faq.a: It works well. It'll also strip whatever sealer is on there, so seal it afterward.

faq.q: Should there be grout in the corners of my shower?
faq.a: No. Corners move and grout cracks when they do. Those joints belong in caulk.
On floors and in showers, yes. It doesn't prevent stains, it gives you time to catch them.
